taif.title: The Day of al-Ta'if: when kindness is met with abuse
subCategories: Patience while working to change reality
participants: Zayd ibn Harithah (may Allah be pleased with him)
taif.eventDescription: After the death of his uncle Abu Talib and his wife Khadijah (may Allah be pleased with her), in what is known as the Year of Sorrow, the Prophet ﷺ went to al-Ta'if to invite its people to Islam and seek their support. They rejected him harshly and set their foolish ones on him, who stoned him until his blessed feet bled, while his servant Zayd ibn Harithah shielded him with his own body.
taif.historicalContext: This happened in the tenth year of the prophethood, at a hard time in the Prophet's ﷺ life after losing his two supports in Makkah, about two years before the migration to Madinah.
taif.problemType: Facing harsh rejection and collective abuse after giving effort and kindness
taif.responseType: Patience, praying for their guidance instead of revenge, and entrusting the matter to Allah
principles: Severe harm does not justify answering abuse with greater abuse
Being able to take revenge does not mean you must use it
Hoping people will change in the future is better than despairing of them
Turning to Allah with your complaint comes before any reaction towards people
modernApplications: If your effort or kindness is harshly rejected, allow yourself to be sad without letting it turn into a desire for revenge
Separate your right to feel angry from making a hasty decision because of it
Think long term: does revenge change the situation, or make it more complicated?
Ask for support from those around you instead of facing the harm alone, as Zayd accompanied the Prophet ﷺ
notToApplyTo: This does not mean staying silent about every injustice; claiming your right is legitimate
“Always forgive” should not be generalised to every case of ongoing harm or physical violence
behaviorObservations: He did not accept the offer of the Angel of the Mountains to destroy the people of al-Ta'if, despite Allah's permission
He turned his anger into a prayer for their guidance, not for their destruction
He did not hide his sadness, but expressed it honestly without losing his balance
He accepted someone to protect him and did not insist on facing the situation alone
whatToAvoid: Confusing “patience” with “accepting continued harm without doing anything”
Believing that everyone who rejects your kindness today will stay that way forever
taif.reflection: This situation shows that true strength is not measured by the ability to take revenge, but by the ability to hold it back when revenge is possible and available.
keywords: insulted me after i helped them
tried to help and was rejected
let down by those i expected support from

hadithRefs.narrator: ‘A'ishah, Mother of the Believers (may Allah be pleased with her)

jabdha-arabi.title: The bedouin's pull: when rudeness is met with a smile
subCategories: Dealing with someone of harsh temperament
participants: Anas ibn Malik (may Allah be pleased with him), the narrator
jabdha-arabi.eventDescription: While the Prophet ﷺ was walking wearing a Najrani cloak with a thick border, a bedouin caught up with him and pulled his cloak so violently that its border left a mark on his blessed neck, then said rudely: “O Muhammad, order for me some of Allah's wealth that you have.” The Prophet ﷺ turned to him and laughed, then ordered that he be given something.
jabdha-arabi.historicalContext: One of many situations in which the Prophet ﷺ dealt with the roughness of some desert Arabs who had not yet learned Islam's manners of speech and conduct.
jabdha-arabi.problemType: Facing rude or rough behaviour from someone who does not necessarily intend harm so much as having a coarse nature
jabdha-arabi.responseType: Forbearance, not answering the act with a similar reaction, and turning the situation into kindness
principles: Not all rudeness is intended harm; it may be a lack of refinement or ignorance of manners
Forbearance when you are able to respond is the hardest and most valuable
You can overlook an offence and also be kind to the one who committed it
modernApplications: Before reacting immediately, ask yourself: does this behaviour come from ill intent or from a lack of manners?
Do not match your reaction to the other person's harshness, but to what befits you
Try making your response better than the other person expected; this is sometimes more powerful than confrontation
notToApplyTo: This level of forbearance is not required in cases of repeated abuse or actual physical violence; those need firmness and self-protection
behaviorObservations: He showed no anger despite the physical pain the pull caused
He met the rude request with giving instead of refusal or rebuke
He laughed instead of frowning, which defused the tension
whatToAvoid: Assuming every rudeness is deliberate harm that deserves immediate boycott or cutting off
jabdha-arabi.reflection: This situation shows that noble character does not stop at treating well those who treat you well; it extends to those who are ill-mannered with you without meaning it.

hadithRefs.narrator: Anas ibn Malik (may Allah be pleased with him)

contrasts: Here he gave up a personal right out of forbearance; there he refused to give up a public right even for the people closest to him — the difference between what one may forgive and what one may not

bawl-arabi.title: The bedouin in the mosque: teaching with gentleness, not harshness
subCategories: Choosing the right time and way to advise
Someone who errs out of ignorance
bawl-arabi.eventDescription: A bedouin entered the Prophet's Mosque and urinated in a corner of it. Some Companions rose to rebuke him harshly, but the Prophet ﷺ said: “Leave him,” and let him finish. Then he ordered a bucket of water to be poured over the urine, and explained the wisdom: “You have been sent to make things easy, not to make them difficult.”
bawl-arabi.historicalContext: One of the best-known situations showing the Prophet's ﷺ gentleness with the ignorant and teaching them without hurting them; it took place in the Prophet's Mosque in Madinah.
bawl-arabi.problemType: Dealing with a mistake made out of ignorance, not to offend
bawl-arabi.responseType: Preventing immediate escalation, then correcting gently right after the situation ended
principles: Hasty correction can cause more harm than the mistake itself
Being gentle with the ignorant does not mean justifying the mistake, but choosing the right time and way to correct it
The religion came to make things easy, not difficult, in dealing with people's mistakes
modernApplications: Do not stop someone in the middle of a mistake with a sharp reaction if that would cause greater harm
Separate the moment of the mistake from the moment of correction; choose the best time to advise
Use a teaching style, not a scolding style, when correcting someone who erred unintentionally
notToApplyTo: This does not apply to deliberate or repeated mistakes made knowingly; those need a different firmness
behaviorObservations: He stopped the Companions from interrupting the bedouin to avoid greater harm
He postponed the correction until right after the situation was over
He explained his guidance through the general wisdom of the religion, not personal criticism
whatToAvoid: Confusing firmness in principle with gentleness in method; the Prophet ﷺ did not approve the act but corrected it gently
bawl-arabi.reflection: This situation teaches us that good teaching is no less important than the correctness of the information being passed on.
keywords: someone made a mistake out of ignorance
my son made a mistake and i don't know how to correct him
how to correct someone without embarrassing them

hadithRefs.narrator: Abu Hurayrah and Anas ibn Malik (may Allah be pleased with them)

tifl-hijr.title: The child in his lap: gentleness even in awkward moments
participants: Umm Qays bint Mihsan (may Allah be pleased with her) and her little son
tifl-hijr.eventDescription: Umm Qays bint Mihsan brought her little son, who was not yet eating food, to the Prophet ﷺ. He sat him in his lap, and the child urinated on his blessed garment. The Prophet ﷺ called for water and sprinkled it over the spot without scrubbing it, and without showing any annoyance that would frighten the mother or the child.
tifl-hijr.historicalContext: One of the hadith describing how the Prophet ﷺ treated infants, usually narrated in the context of the rulings on an infant's urine.
tifl-hijr.problemType: Dealing with an annoying, unintended act by a small child
tifl-hijr.responseType: Not showing annoyance, and handling the situation calmly
emotionsAddressed: A parent's anxiety about an embarrassing moment
principles: A child is not judged by adult standards
Calm in handling children's embarrassing moments keeps everyone at ease
Welcoming children warmly is not contradicted by occasional uncomfortable moments
modernApplications: Do not let your reaction to a child's unintended behaviour be bigger than the situation
Deal with the consequence calmly without making the child or their parent feel extra embarrassment
Remember that your kind welcome of children may stay in their parents' memory for a long time
behaviorObservations: He showed no irritation or displeasure in front of the mother
He chose the lightest way to deal with it (sprinkling, not a full wash)
He kept welcoming mothers and their children despite such moments
whatToAvoid: Comparing a child's behaviour with what is expected of an adult
tifl-hijr.reflection: In this outwardly small situation lies a great meaning: a big heart is measured in simple daily details as much as in major events.
keywords: embarrassed by my child in front of people

hadithRefs.narrator: Umm Qays bint Mihsan (may Allah be pleased with her)

khidmat-anas.title: Ten years of service: the character of one who never scolded
participants: Anas ibn Malik (may Allah be pleased with him)
khidmat-anas.eventDescription: Anas ibn Malik served the Prophet ﷺ for ten full years from a young age, and he testified: “I served the Messenger of Allah ﷺ for ten years, and he never once said ‘uff’ to me, nor said of anything I had done, ‘Why did you do that?’, nor of anything I had not done, ‘Why didn't you do that?’”
khidmat-anas.historicalContext: This testimony describes the Prophet's ﷺ daily manner with the one who served him over ten continuous years.
prophetTraits: Fairness to those under his authority
khidmat-anas.problemType: Dealing with people under your responsibility or authority (an employee, someone younger or weaker in position)
khidmat-anas.responseType: Not complaining, and leaving unnecessary questioning over small details
emotionsAddressed: Frustration with the performance of those under your responsibility
The urge to monitor every detail
principles: Whoever has authority over others is required to show more self-control, not less
Not holding people to account for small things builds a long-term relationship based on trust
Exemplary character is built through daily repetition, not only in exceptional moments
modernApplications: If you are responsible for others at work or at home, avoid questioning every small detail
Before complaining about someone's performance, remember how long you have worked together and the whole picture, not one moment
Keep a calm tone even in situations that provoke you every day
notToApplyTo: This does not mean no accountability at all at work; it concerns the daily way of dealing with small, non-essential mistakes
behaviorObservations: He never voiced irritation through ten full years
He did not hold Anas to account for his small actions or omissions
He kept this manner consistently, not in one passing moment
whatToAvoid: Thinking that good character with those who serve you is weak management
khidmat-anas.reflection: This simple testimony gives a complete picture of character tested in small, repeated details, not only on big occasions.
keywords: i shout at people who work with me

hadithRefs.narrator: Anas ibn Malik (may Allah be pleased with him)

la-taghdab.title: “Do not get angry”: advice that sums up all wisdom
participants: A Companion (said to be Jariyah ibn Qudamah, or Abu al-Darda')
la-taghdab.eventDescription: A man came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: “Advise me.” He said: “Do not get angry.” The man repeated his request several times, asking for other advice, and each time the answer was: “Do not get angry.”
la-taghdab.historicalContext: One of the Prophet's concise, comprehensive sayings, in the form of short all-encompassing advice.
la-taghdab.problemType: Asking for practical advice on a recurring character problem such as a quick temper
la-taghdab.responseType: Focusing on the root of the problem instead of listing scattered tips
principles: Some comprehensive advice is more useful than many scattered tips
Anger is the root of many other problems, so controlling it treats many problems at once
Repeating the same advice may be the right cure for a particular person
modernApplications: If you are looking for lots of tips to improve your behaviour, start by controlling your anger; it may solve a large part of the problem
Before taking any decision or saying anything in a moment of anger, give yourself time to calm down
Notice the patterns: do most of your problems start with a moment of uncontrolled anger?
behaviorObservations: He did not answer with a long list of instructions despite the man's insistence
He repeated the same answer without tiring, because he saw it as the right cure for this particular person
whatToAvoid: Believing that lots of advice matters more than applying one essential piece of advice
la-taghdab.reflection: Sometimes the problem is not a lack of knowledge, but not applying the one principle everyone already knows.
keywords: someone insulted me and i want to pay them back
someone humiliated me and i want revenge
i want to prove i'm stronger

quranRefs.context: Among the qualities of the pious described in the Quran; commentators (including al-Qurtubi) linked this verse to the hadith on controlling anger
quranRefs.relevance: It makes restraining anger and pardoning people a quality of faith that Allah loves, not merely good social behaviour

hadithRefs.narrator: Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him)

laysa-shadid.title: True strength: self-control, not overpowering others
participants: Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), the narrator
laysa-shadid.eventDescription: The Prophet ﷺ set a different standard for strength when he said: “The strong one is not the one who overcomes people by wrestling; the strong one is the one who controls himself when angry,” showing that physical strength and the ability to overpower others are not the true measure of strength.
laysa-shadid.historicalContext: One of his concise sayings ﷺ that redefine common moral ideas.
laysa-shadid.problemType: Redefining strength and victory in a moment of anger
laysa-shadid.responseType: Shifting the idea of “winning” from physical or verbal dominance to self-control
emotionsAddressed: The urge to prove strength by retorting or overpowering
Feeling that not responding is weakness
principles: Controlling yourself when angry is harder and nobler than physical dominance
In many situations the real victory is over yourself, not over the opponent
Strength of personality has nothing to do with a sharp reaction
modernApplications: The next time you feel angry and want to assert yourself forcefully, remember that control is the real strength, not impulse
Do not confuse “not responding sharply” with “weakness”; they are completely different
Measure your success in the situation by how much you stayed in control, not by how much you beat the other person
behaviorObservations: He redefined “strength” away from its usual physical meaning
whatToAvoid: Thinking that every refusal to respond sharply is weakness of character
laysa-shadid.reflection: When strength is measured by something other than dominance, self-control becomes the hardest and most beautiful victory.
keywords: i want to prove i'm stronger
i won't back down so i don't look weak
i feel that staying silent is weakness
someone insulted me in public and i want to respond the same way

quranRefs.context: Among the qualities of the pious described in the Quran; commentators (including al-Qurtubi) linked it to the hadith “The strong one is not the wrestler”
quranRefs.relevance: It describes restraining anger as a quality of the doers of good whom Allah loves, confirming that self-control is a virtue, not just an ability

hadithRefs.narrator: Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him)

adl-fatima.title: Justice without favouritism: “Even if Fatimah stole”
participants: Usamah ibn Zayd (may Allah be pleased with him)
adl-fatima.eventDescription: A woman from a tribe of high social standing who had stolen was brought to the Prophet ﷺ. Some tried to intercede for her through Usamah ibn Zayd. The Prophet's ﷺ face changed and he said: “Do you intercede regarding one of the limits set by Allah?” Then he addressed the people, explaining that the nations before them were destroyed because they applied the punishment to the weak and left the noble. He said: “By the One in whose hand is my soul, if Fatimah the daughter of Muhammad stole, I would cut off her hand.”
adl-fatima.historicalContext: This took place during the conquest of Makkah, and it is one of the clearest texts on the principle of equality before what is right, regardless of social standing.
adl-fatima.problemType: Pressure to exempt someone from a general rule because of their status or closeness
adl-fatima.responseType: Refusing favouritism, and applying the same standard to everyone, including those closest to him
emotionsAddressed: Feeling wronged when seeing favouritism towards the powerful
Social pressure to be lenient with those close to you
principles: True justice is tested when it concerns those closest to you, not strangers
Favouring people of status is a direct cause of the collapse of justice in any society
Kinship or friendship should not be a reason to suspend a right or a general rule
modernApplications: If you are in a position of responsibility, apply the same rules to those close to you as to everyone else
Beware of social pressure pushing you to be lenient with the powerful or relatives at the expense of justice
If you see favouritism from others, remember that demanding justice is a legitimate right
notToApplyTo: This situation illustrates the principle of justice and equality; it should not be used to decide detailed legal rulings on punishments without referring to a qualified scholar
behaviorObservations: His blessed face changed when he was asked to intercede in something contrary to justice
He addressed the matter publicly with a sermon, not only privately
He gave the example of the person closest to him to remove any doubt that the rule was general, without exception
whatToAvoid: Using this text to justify disproportionate harshness; the point is equality, not severity
adl-fatima.reflection: When the one in authority uses the person closest to him as the example, the word “justice” becomes more than a slogan.

quranRefs.context: An explicit Quranic command to uphold justice even against oneself, one's parents or closest relatives
quranRefs.relevance: It establishes the same principle the hadith embodied in practice: no one is exempt from justice, whatever their kinship or status

hadithRefs.narrator: ‘A'ishah, Mother of the Believers (may Allah be pleased with her)

contrasts: Here he refused to give up a public right even for the person closest to him; there he gave up a personal right out of forbearance — the difference between what one may forgive and what one may not

fath-makkah.title: “Go, you are free”: forgiveness at the height of power
fath-makkah.eventDescription: After the Prophet ﷺ entered Makkah victorious, its people stood waiting to see what he would do to them after years of harm, war and driving him from his home. He asked them: “What do you think I will do with you?” They answered: “A noble brother, and the son of a noble brother.” He said: “Go, for you are free.”
fath-makkah.historicalContext: The conquest of Makkah took place in the eighth year after the migration, one of the greatest moments of empowerment in the Prophet's biography.
fath-makkah.problemType: How to act on gaining full power to take revenge on former oppressors
fath-makkah.responseType: A general amnesty instead of revenge, despite every justification for revenge
emotionsAddressed: The desire for revenge after reaching a position of strength
Feeling that victory deserves a price from the defeated side
principles: True forgiveness shows at the moment of full power to retaliate, not at the moment of helplessness
Victory does not require humiliating the defeated
Tolerance after gaining power can send a stronger message than punishment
modernApplications: When you reach a position of strength over someone who harmed you before, ask yourself: does revenge achieve a real goal, or satisfy a passing feeling?
Distinguish between claiming your right and humiliating the one who wronged you once you are in the stronger position
Tolerance after gaining power is a stronger message than tolerance when you are helpless
notToApplyTo: This does not mean giving up public rights or not holding to account those whose actions affected the rights of others
Forgiveness here was a personal choice of the one in authority, not a rule that cancels public justice
behaviorObservations: He did not offer the people of Makkah a choice between punishment and pardon; he pardoned them straight away
He used a question rather than a direct verdict, giving them a chance to reflect
The pardon was not accompanied by repeated reminders of past wrongs
whatToAvoid: Confusing personal forgiveness of a wrong against you with leniency regarding other people's public rights
fath-makkah.reflection: One of the beautiful paradoxes is that the greatest moment of power in the Prophet's biography was used not for revenge, but for forgiveness.
keywords: i'm now in a position of power over the one who wronged me
the person who mistreated me is now under my authority
should i take revenge or forgive now that i won
i have the upper hand over someone who used to oppress me

hudaybiyyah.title: The Treaty of al-Hudaybiyah: wisdom in accepting terms that seem harsh
subCategories: Trusting Allah while taking the means
participants: ‘Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him)
Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him)
hudaybiyyah.eventDescription: The Prophet ﷺ and his Companions set out for ‘umrah, but Quraysh prevented them from entering Makkah. A treaty was negotiated whose terms seemed unfair to the Muslims, which upset some Companions, including ‘Umar ibn al-Khattab, who questioned the Prophet ﷺ about it. The Muslims pledged allegiance to the Prophet ﷺ under the tree to stand firm at that critical moment, in what became known as the Pledge of Ridwan.
hudaybiyyah.historicalContext: These events took place in the sixth year after the migration, and the Quran later called this treaty a “victory” because of the openness to the message that followed.
prophetTraits: Trusting Allah while taking the means
hudaybiyyah.problemType: Making a decision that looks like a concession or a loss, but is in fact far-sighted wisdom
hudaybiyyah.responseType: Standing firm on the decision while understanding the objections of those close to him, without being drawn into an emotional decision
emotionsAddressed: Frustration with a decision that seems unfair
The urge to face the situation by force instead of negotiating
principles: Not every result that looks like a loss is a real loss in the long run
Accepting unsatisfying terms is sometimes part of a larger strategy for a wider benefit
Listening to the objections of those close to you does not necessarily mean changing the right decision
modernApplications: Before rejecting an agreement or decision that seems entirely unfair, study the wider picture and the long-term results
If you are in a leadership position, listen respectfully to objections around you even if you decide to go ahead
Do not judge a decision's success only by how you feel about it in the first moment
notToApplyTo: This does not mean accepting any unjust condition without thinking; the decision here came after negotiation and study, not absolute surrender
behaviorObservations: He did not change his decision because of ‘Umar's objection, despite ‘Umar's standing
He carried out the terms of the treaty in practice so that his Companions would be reassured
He did not punish those who objected, but met their objection with an open heart
whatToAvoid: Thinking that everyone who objects to a leader's decision deserves blame; the objection here came from concern, not disobedience
hudaybiyyah.reflection: Sometimes the wise decision is the one that does not look wise at the time, and this only becomes clear once time reveals what lay behind it.
keywords: a hard decision that seems unfair
should i accept terms i don't like
a leadership decision not everyone understands
hard decision i don't know what to do

quranRefs.context: Revealed about the Pledge of Ridwan made during the negotiations at al-Hudaybiyah
quranRefs.relevance: It shows that standing firm with the leader in critical moments with unclear outcomes has great value with Allah

hadithRefs.narrator: Several narrators, including al-Miswar ibn Makhramah and Marwan ibn al-Hakam
